judgments.reasoning_cat1: The fee formula is precise, but "payable only as interest with respect to such Loan is received" and the diversion of "components of the Loan Servicing Fee" paid directly by borrowers to the Servicer are loosely expressed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The direct-payment carve-out lets the Servicer take fees outside the Company's books, which sits against the aggregate compensation cap in 5.3(f) that is measured by the fees "payable" under 5.4(b)-(f).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, arithmetically definite entitlement to ten percent of late charges.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is one of the capped items under 5.3(f); no conflict identified.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "The regular state interest rate payable to the Company under the Portfolio Loan" is opaque — "state" appears to be an error for "stated", and the benchmark is otherwise unidentifiable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It feeds the 5.3(f) compensation cap, so an unreadable benchmark makes that cap harder to apply, but no direct conflict appears.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line entitlement to enumerated borrower-paid fees; concrete.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps with the "Loan Origination Fee" in 5.7(a), which is likewise a brokerage/origination/renewal/forbearance fee, raising a question which provision governs the same payment.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single short item, definite in scope.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the 5.3(f) cap list; nothing contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "All costs, fees, and expenses incurred ... in connection with the formation, organization, reorganization, operation and general administration" plus "any extraordinary expenses" is a broad general category whose boundary against the excluded "Loan Services" expenses is imprecise.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The exclusion depends on the definition of Loan Services in 5.3(f), and the indemnification reference is to the Operating Agreement rather than to 5.5(c), so the expense allocation between Company, Manager and Servicer must be pieced together across provisions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Short and clear, though it defines "Permitted Expenses" as "the foregoing expenses and indemnifications" when the preceding text mentions indemnification only in passing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: "Permitted Expenses" is defined here but appears nowhere else in the Agreement, and the indemnifications it purports to capture are set out in 5.5(c) and the Operating Agreement.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The exculpation is mis-fitted: it indemnifies "members, officers, employees, and consultants of the Company" but the carve-out is measured by misconduct "in performing or in failing to perform the Manager's duties under the operating agreement", so the standard does not match the class.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is discretionary indemnification by the Manager for the Manager's own affiliates while 4.3 disclaims all fiduciary duty, and it interacts with 5.5(a)'s inclusion of indemnification expenses as Company Expenses.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Any construction, brokerage, property management or development or similar compensation" is a specific list closed by an undefined catch-all, and the sentence runs on for many lines with nested parentheticals.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It permits the Manager to keep fees outside the 5.4 compensation schedule and the 5.3(f) cap, which is exactly the sort of leakage those provisions appear designed to control.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "In an amount determined on a case-by-case basis" fixes no limit at all, and the sentence's pronoun "it" leaves ambiguous which of the Company, Manager, Servicer or Affiliate receives the fee.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 5.6 says any Loan Origination Fee remains the Manager's property, so the ambiguity about the recipient is resolved against the Company — but that in turn sits against 5.4's closed compensation schedule.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The clause enumerates conditions (i)-(iii) and then in (iv) disapplies all of them for Sponsored Investment Funds and Private Clients, and the numbering is muddled (subclauses labelled (1)/(i) and (ii) within (ii)); "commercially reasonable efforts" and "fair price on the open market" are elastic.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The (iv) carve-out lets affiliated funds and clients buy foreclosed property free of the protections, which is hard to reconcile with 5.7(e)'s related-party regime and with 5.3(d)'s general sale power.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Condition (i) reads "the borrower shall not be default under the loan", a mechanical omission, and (iii) turns on "loan underwriting criteria customarily applied by the Company", an internal and unverifiable standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This provision is the specific control on affiliate loan purchases, yet 5.3(e) purports to allow purchases from the same counterparties "on such terms and conditions as the Manager, in its sole discretion, determines", and 5.7(e) exempts Sponsored Investment Fund and Private Client loans from the related-party regime altogether.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The pricing floor (greater of unpaid balance or fair market value) is definite, though "other charges owing under such loan" is undefined.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cross-refers to 5.7(e)(iii)'s buy-back obligation and stands against 5.3(e)'s general sole-discretion sale power, so which governs a sale to a Sponsored Investment Fund is contestable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The prohibition is defined by reference to whether the borrower "is an Affiliate", and then the closing paragraph excludes any loan whose borrower is a Sponsored Investment Fund or Private Client — a specific carve-out that largely swallows the general rule and leaves its reach uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with the 5.1(a) Affiliate definition (which excludes Noteholders) and the 5.1(c) definition naming R.E. Loans as a Sponsored Investment Fund, the twenty percent cap and buy-back protections do not apply to the most obvious affiliated borrowers — a genuine incoherence with 4.3 and 5.7(a)-(d).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two clear conditions, arm's-length terms and lien subordination; "no less favorable to the Company than terms negotiated in an arm's length transaction" is a familiar standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Condition (ii) requires Advance liens to be junior to the Lien securing the Notes, which is consistent with 2.3(b) and 5.3(a)'s ordering of Company Borrowings.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The arm's-length comparator ("in the same geographical market with comparable property as security") is a soft standard, but the structure is clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its final sentence speaks of "Noteholders who are also Affiliates of the Manager or Servicer" although 5.1(a) expressly provides that "Affiliate" shall not include any Noteholder — a direct definitional conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A broad but conventional outside-activities waiver; "no provision of this Agreement shall be deemed to prohibit" is sweeping but plain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The sweeping override clashes with the actual prohibitions in 5.7(b)-(e) and 6.2, which do restrict the Manager's and its affiliates' dealings, so the two must be harmonised.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "At such times as the Company has not repaid in full" is an awkward temporal formulation but its sense is clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sets a simple majority consent override for all Section 6 covenants, whereas 6.1 states its covenants unconditionally and 6.2 uses the defined "Majority in Interest" threshold — overlapping and slightly different consent mechanics.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short lead-in; the heading in the body reads "Affirmative Covenants" while the table of contents says "Affirmative Covenant", a trivial slip.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It omits the consent override stated in the Section 6 chapeau, so read literally the 6.1 covenants are absolute while the chapeau makes them waivable by majority consent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Promptly" is the only soft word in an otherwise definite perfection covenant.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The perfection duty is undercut by 5.3(a) and 2.3(b), which permit senior liens and subordination of the Lien the Company must perfect.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Clear ratable payment covenant with an express carve-out for the prepayment discretion.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It restates 1.4(c) but measures ratability by "aggregate principal and interest amounts payable" rather than by relative principal amounts, a small but real inconsistency between the two payment rules.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Such amount of their business time ... as is reasonably necessary to effectively manage the affairs" is a vague and essentially unenforceable time commitment.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its vagueness is compounded by 5.9, which expressly permits the Manager's principals to devote time to other businesses and Sponsored Investment Funds.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Concrete accounting and audit obligations; "reasonable time" and "reasonable advance notice" are ordinary qualifiers, and the alternative GAAP/IFRS election is expressly the Company's.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It grants inspection rights to "Members and Noteholders" although 4.3 states Purchasers do not become members; that is a harmless overlap rather than a conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The reporting obligation beyond tax information is entirely discretionary ("as the Company, in its discretion, may determine"), which makes limb (b) close to illusory.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits 1.2(a)'s optional website posting of Loan Amount information; no contradiction found.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Commercially reasonable efforts" plus a list ending in "or other security" leaves an open-ended catch-all in a securities-law-sensitive covenant.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It qualifies the Co-Lending Activities authorised in 5.3(c) and 5.8; the two read together coherently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: As written this affirmative covenant obliges the Company "To make any mortgage loan, if ... [foreign Portfolio Loans] exceed[] twenty percent" — plainly an omitted negative, so the text states the opposite of what was intended.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The intended twenty percent foreign cap is what makes sense of 3.7's "located primarily in the United States" purpose, so the missing negative also puts this covenant at odds with the rest of the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line catch-all performance covenant; nothing ambiguous in it.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It references the Subscription Agreement, Notes and Security Agreement, all identified in 10.7, so the document set is consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It defines "Majority in Interest" by a numeric threshold; clear, apart from the capitalised but undefined "Principal balances".
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Section 6 chapeau already imposed a majority-consent override in different words, and 1.5 uses yet another >50% formulation for amending the Notes.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, definite negative covenant.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It bars voluntary liquidation without consent while 1.6 contemplates extending maturity for an "orderly liquidation of Portfolio Loans" — a mild tension only, since liquidating loans is not dissolving the Company.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It borrows "Lien" and "Collateral" from the Security Agreement while 2.3(b) defines "Lien" differently in this Agreement, so the same capitalised term carries two meanings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The carve-out for Company Borrowings makes the prohibition largely inoperative given 5.3(a)'s broad authority to grant senior liens and subordination, and the duty to "defend the Collateral against" such Liens is hard to square with that authority.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The prohibition is short but odd: it bars paying "any salaries or bonuses" directly in any month a management fee is payable, without saying to whom.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It keys to a "Portfolio Management Fee", a term never defined — 5.4(a) defines the "Management Fee" — so the trigger for the prohibition is uncertain on the face of the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Settle any claim that the Company may have against a Member" is clear, though the parenthetical exclusion of Sponsored Investment Funds is unexplained.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The carve-out for Sponsored Investment Funds echoes the pattern in 5.7(b)(iv) and 5.7(e) of exempting affiliated funds from noteholder protections, reinforcing the same structural question.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single short prohibition; unambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It presupposes a possible plurality of Managers, consistent with the 3.3 definition of "Manager" as the manager or managers.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Materially and adversely effects" uses the wrong word, and "economic interests of the Noteholders" is a soft threshold that the Company itself would judge.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The preamble incorporates the Operating Agreement "as it may be amended from time to time" and 5.2 lets proceeds be used for any purpose not prohibited by that agreement, so amendments to it have direct effect here despite this restriction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It bars assignment "or delegation" of a Note and calls the Notes "non-negotiable", and it conditions transfer on the transferee being a "qualified investor", a term never defined.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 8.1(b) contemplates the Manager filing instruments to effect a Noteholder's assignment of a Note and 1.7 contemplates re-issue on transfer, so transfers are anticipated notwithstanding the flat prohibition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The grant is broad — "any certificates, instruments and documents, as may be required by, or may be appropriate under" — and clause (iii) reads "comply with state or federal securities", omitting "laws".
judgments.reasoning_cat2: An irrevocable power to execute "any amendments or cancellation" of this Agreement and the Security Agreement in the Noteholder's name is difficult to reconcile with the consent thresholds in 1.5 and 10.5 and with 4.3's creditor-only relationship.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The sentence's final purpose clause ("for the sole purpose of enabling the Manager to ... effect such transfer") sits ambiguously — it may qualify only survival on assignment or the whole grant.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read with Section 7, which forbids assignment without consent, the survival-on-assignment language addresses a transfer the Agreement generally prohibits.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "Necessary or expedient" and "necessary or appropriate in the judgment of the Manager" are broad but standard further-assurance formulations.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly cumulative with the 8.1 power of attorney and consistent with 4.2.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "The Manager will appoint" leaves timing entirely open, and the priority-of-payment sentence is convoluted about when the Collateral Agent is paid ahead of the Noteholders.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: A Collateral Agent appointed and replaceable by the Manager, whose actions bind Noteholders, is in tension with 4.3's creditor-only relationship and with 5.3(a)'s power to direct the Collateral Agent to subordinate the Lien.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: "On terms required by Manager" combined with "only to the extent that such terms or actions are not prohibited under this Agreement" is internally awkward — the agent must do the Manager's bidding but only within limits stated elsewhere.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The limit refers back to 5.3(a), which prohibits almost nothing, so the qualifier gives Noteholders little protection; that interplay is the natural site of a dispute.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The substitution right is definite, though "during any period that the Company is in default under the Notes" is not tied to any defined event of default in this Agreement.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Agreement contains no default or acceleration provisions at all, so the trigger for the Noteholder consent right must be sourced from the Notes or Security Agreement, which are not before the reader.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard successors-and-assigns and no-third-party-beneficiary language.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 7 forbids assignment of the Notes without consent, and Section 9 arguably confers rights on a Collateral Agent who is not a party, so the no-third-party clause has some friction, softened by its own "except as expressly provided" proviso.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional Delaware choice-of-law clause, definite on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 10.8(d) invokes the California Rules of Professional Conduct and 5.1(c)/5.3(f) name California entities, so a Delaware-only governing law sits a little oddly with the document's California orientation.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Pure boilerplate with no room for construction.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing elsewhere addresses execution formalities differently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clear list of delivery methods and deemed-receipt times; it omits any address block or place for notice, which is a gap rather than an ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 10.5 lets the Company waive "any notice provision" in its discretion, which qualifies this clause but is expressly stated.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The paragraph mixes several rules — collective modification, individual Noteholder modification, unilateral Company waiver of timing provisions — and "effective with respect to all Purchasers" leaves open whether a non-conforming modification binds some parties.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps and does not perfectly align with 1.5, which sets a different consent formula for amending the Notes and adds a protection against discriminatory amendments.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard non-waiver and cumulative-remedies language, long but conventional.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It speaks of Noteholders' remedies although 5.3(a) authorises standstill and subordination agreements restricting exactly those remedies and Section 9 vests enforcement in a Collateral Agent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An ordinary integration clause naming the constituent documents.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The preamble incorporates the Operating Agreement's definitions and 4.1(b) relies on a private placement memorandum, neither of which is listed here — a real question whether those documents are inside or outside the integrated agreement.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long recital of counsel's roles with a missing closing quotation mark and a stray reference to "Each Investor" although the parties are defined as Purchasers and Noteholders.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The word "Investor" is used here and in 5.7(e) though never defined, and the Agreement's parties are Purchasers/Noteholders, so the class bound by this acknowledgement is imprecise.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short, categorical statement that counsel does not represent the Noteholders.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with 10.8(c) and (d) and with 4.3's creditor-only relationship.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Clear allocation of the Noteholder's own counsel costs; "except as otherwise specifically provided by this Agreement" is an unspecified saving clause.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 9(a) gives the Collateral Agent priority payment of counsel costs from the Collateral, which is the exception this clause gestures at without naming.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It waives only "any present conflict of interest" while the consent is expressed as covering "any and all Company Legal Matters" including future disputes — a genuine present/future mismatch in the same sentence.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 10.9 then gives consents to future and unrelated representations, so the two conflict-waiver provisions must be read together to determine the waiver's temporal reach.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Dense but conventional informed-consent language; the closing sentence about the Rules of Conduct is explanatory rather than operative.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It supplements 10.8(d) and is subject to the same Rules of Conduct override; no conflict identified.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It uses "Portfolio Loan Transaction", a term not defined (10.8(a) defines "Portfolio Transactions"), and the final consent is made "subject to the specific consent" of the same party who is giving consent, which is circular.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The definitional slip against 10.8(a) and the reliance on the Sponsored Investment Fund definition in 5.1(c) mean the scope of the consent depends on terms defined elsewhere and imperfectly matched.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The paragraph repeats "with their permission" three times and is convoluted, but the consent it seeks is intelligible.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It states counsel represented solely the Company and Sponsored Investment Funds in the Transactions, consistent with 10.8(b) and 10.9(a).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A standard restrictive legend; its terms (effective registration statement or satisfactory opinion of counsel) are definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Section 7 imposes a stricter and differently worded transfer bar (Company consent in sole discretion, qualified investors only), so the legend and the operative transfer clause do not state the same condition.
